prompt: In the store fixture, when does the code after yield run?

choices.text: Before the test, as part of setup
choices.why: Setup is the part before yield.

choices.text: After the test, passed or failed alike
choices.why: Right. Teardown runs either way, so the connection is closed even after a failure.

choices.text: After the test, and only when it passed
choices.why: A failing assertion does not skip the fixture's teardown.

choices.text: Once at the end of the whole session
choices.why: That would be a session-scoped fixture; this one is per function.

prompt: In the --setup-show run of the three store tests, how many times was the store fixture set up?
Why is a close() at the end of a test body less reliable than teardown after yield?

choices.text: Because close() is slower inside a test
choices.why: Speed is not the issue.

choices.text: Because pytest deletes the test body after it runs
choices.why: pytest deletes nothing of the kind.

choices.text: A failed assertion stops the test before the close
choices.why: Right. Lines after the failing assert are skipped; the fixture's teardown is not.

choices.text: Because SQLite refuses a close from test code
choices.why: SQLite does not know who calls close.

prompt: A fixture defined in a file named ___ is available to every test file beside it without an import.
The store fixture was made module-scoped while still asking for tmp_path. What did pytest do?

choices.text: Refused it: ScopeMismatch
choices.why: Right. A module fixture cannot depend on a function fixture it would outlive.

choices.text: Ran the tests, each sharing one tmp_path
choices.why: It never got that far.

choices.text: Silently widened tmp_path to module scope
choices.why: pytest does not change a fixture's scope for you.

choices.text: Skipped the store tests with a warning
choices.why: It reported errors, not skips.

prompt: With the module-scoped store, test_a_new_store_has_no_quotes failed in the full file and passed alone. Why?

choices.text: Because -k runs tests with a fresh Python
choices.why: It is the same interpreter; the difference is what ran before.

choices.text: Earlier tests had filled the shared store
choices.why: Right. Alone, nothing ran before it, so the store was empty.

choices.text: Because recent is broken for ten rows
choices.why: recent works; the store simply was not empty.

choices.text: Because the CHECK constraint failed in that test
choices.why: That test inserts nothing.

prompt: In that run, how many ids did the shared store hold when the new test read it?
hint: The failed CHECK insert wrote nothing.

prompt: When is widening a fixture's scope safe, by the lesson's rule? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: It is measurably expensive to build
choices.why: Right. That is the first condition.

choices.text: Tests cannot change it, or each undoes its changes
choices.why: Right. That is the second condition.

choices.text: It is used by more than three tests
choices.why: A count of users says nothing about shared state.

choices.text: The tests that use it currently pass
choices.why: They passed in the capture too, until one was added.

prompt: How many quotes.db files did the three store tests leave under pytest-current?

choices.text: One, shared by the three tests
choices.why: Each test had its own directory.

choices.text: Three, one per test directory
choices.why: Right. One database per test, none shared.

choices.text: None; tmp_path is deleted at once
choices.why: pytest keeps the last three runs on purpose.

choices.text: Six, because each test also keeps a backup
choices.why: There are no backups.

prompt: Why does pytest keep the last three runs' directories instead of deleting them at once?

choices.text: To make the next run faster by reusing files
choices.why: Each run starts with new, empty directories.

choices.text: Because deleting files during a run is not allowed by Linux
choices.why: Linux allows it; this is a choice.

choices.text: So a failed test's files are still there to inspect
choices.why: Right. And older runs are deleted, so the disk does not fill up.

choices.text: So that tests of different users share data
choices.why: The directory is per user, which keeps them apart.

prompt: Match each shared resource with its per-test version.
Which design breaks when the code under test commits on its own?

choices.text: One transaction per test, rolled back
choices.why: Right. A commit inside the code ends the transaction the fixture meant to roll back.

choices.text: A fresh schema per test run
choices.why: That design catches commit-time behaviour.

choices.text: Tests that only look at their own rows
choices.why: Commits do not hurt tests that read only their own rows.

choices.text: A separate SQLite file per test
choices.why: Each file is its own database, and commits stay inside it.

prompt: Why does this repository's CLAUDE.md forbid seeding a fixed unique value in a test?

choices.text: Because unique indexes slow PostgreSQL down
choices.why: Speed is not the argument.

choices.text: Because fixed values are a security risk
choices.why: The rule is about collisions, not secrets.

choices.text: Because go test refuses to insert the same value twice
choices.why: The database refuses it, and only when two packages race.

choices.text: Two packages running in parallel collide on the unique index
choices.why: Right. Which one loses is a matter of timing.

prompt: Scope every assertion to the rows the test wrote: WHERE tenant_id = $1, not count( ___ ).
What does a_quote(cep="0131010") return?

choices.text: An error, because the CEP is invalid
choices.why: The factory does not validate; the database does, later.

choices.text: The default quote, with that CEP
choices.why: Right. Overrides replace defaults; the rest stays valid.

choices.text: A quote with only a cep field
choices.why: The other three fields keep their defaults.

choices.text: The id of a saved row
choices.why: The factory builds a dictionary; store.save writes it.

prompt: Why does the factory build created_at from a counter?

choices.text: To match the real time the test ran
choices.why: It is a fixed date with a varying minute, not the real time.

choices.text: Because SQLite requires unique timestamps
choices.why: SQLite has no such rule; the store sorts by it.

choices.text: So two quotes built in a row never share one
choices.why: Right. The store sorts by created_at, so ties would make order depend on the id.

choices.text: To make each run of the suite produce different data
choices.why: The counter restarts every run; the data is the same each time.

prompt: A carrier column is added to quotes. How many store tests have to change, with the factory in place?

choices.text: All three, because each saves a quote
choices.why: Each saves through a_quote, which gets one new default.

choices.text: None
choices.why: Right. Only a test about carriers would name the new field.

choices.text: Only the CHECK test
choices.why: The CHECK test is about the CEP.

choices.text: Two, the ones that compare ids
choices.why: Comparing ids does not involve the new column.

prompt: What is a mystery guest?

choices.text: A test that nobody remembers writing
choices.why: Authorship is not the issue.

choices.text: A fixture that runs without being requested
choices.why: Fixtures run when named; the term is about data.

choices.text: Hidden data the result depends on
choices.why: Right. The test passes and nobody can tell why its expected value is right.

choices.text: A user account created only for testing
choices.why: That is test data, not the smell.

prompt: Match each kind of value with where it belongs.
test_heavy_parcel uses a_quote() with no overrides and asserts 2190. The factory's default weight changes to 800 g for another test. What happens?
hint: 800 g is one extra band, not two.

choices.text: Nothing; the factory is only used by store tests
choices.why: This test uses it too, and depends on its weight.

choices.text: It fails, for a reason none of its own lines show
choices.why: Right. 800 g costs 1740, and the 1200 g it relied on lived in another file.

choices.text: It passes, since 800 g and 1200 g are in the same band
choices.why: 800 g is one extra band, 1200 g two.

choices.text: pytest warns that the factory changed
choices.why: pytest knows nothing about factories.

prompt: When zone N's base went from 2990 to 3090, how many rows of the published table failed?
The table test fails after a price change in the code. What does the failure establish?

choices.text: That the code is wrong and must be reverted
choices.why: Maybe the change was intended and the table is what must move.

choices.text: That the CSV is wrong and must be regenerated
choices.why: Regenerating without reading accepts whatever the code does.

choices.text: That code and table disagree
choices.why: Right. The test cannot know; it stops the two drifting apart silently.

choices.text: That the carrier changed its prices
choices.why: The table is the shop's, not the carrier's.

prompt: Why keep the shop's table in a CSV rather than a list inside the test?

choices.text: The team that owns the numbers can review it
choices.why: Right. A file the business opens keeps the promise and the code in one place.

choices.text: CSV files are parsed faster than Python lists
choices.why: Speed is not the reason.

choices.text: parametrize only accepts data from files
choices.why: Lesson 1 passed it a list.

choices.text: So the tests can be skipped when the file is absent
choices.why: A missing file would be an error, not a skip.

prompt: Expected output stored beside the code and compared on every run is often called a golden file or a ___ .
What does the lesson call a test that passes or fails with no change in between?

choices.text: Skipped
choices.why: A skipped test does not run.

choices.text: Flaky
choices.why: Right. It trains everybody to re-run until green.

choices.text: Golden
choices.why: A golden file is stored expected output.

choices.text: Parametrised
choices.why: That is one test run over many rows.

prompt: Why does dispatch_date take the moment as an argument instead of reading the clock?

choices.text: Because reading the clock is slow in Python
choices.why: It is fast; the problem is that it changes.

choices.text: Because datetime.now cannot take a time zone
choices.why: It can; that is not the reason.

choices.text: Because the HTTP layer has no clock
choices.why: The outer layer is exactly where the real clock is read.

choices.text: So tests give the same answer at any hour
choices.why: Right. The clock becomes an input, like the carrier in lesson 2.

prompt: Which of these are sources of non-determinism the lesson names? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Iterating over a set
choices.why: Right. Its order is not guaranteed.

choices.text: Reading os.environ without the test setting it
choices.why: Right. The answer depends on the machine.

choices.text: Comparing two integers with ==
choices.why: Integer comparison is exact.

choices.text: random without a fixed seed
choices.why: Right. Different numbers each run.

prompt: Against the naive split, what smallest failing input did Hypothesis report?

choices.text: 10000 cents in 3 instalments
choices.why: That is lesson 1's example, which the naive version splits into 3333, 3333, 3334.

choices.text: 2 cents in 4 instalments
choices.why: Right. round(0.5) is 0, so the parts are 0, 0, 0 and 2.

choices.text: 0 cents in 1 instalment
choices.why: That splits into [0], which holds both properties.

choices.text: 1 cent in 24 instalments
choices.why: Hypothesis shrank to a smaller example than that.

prompt: Why did the sum property still pass against the naive split?

choices.text: Because Hypothesis only tried totals divisible by the parts
choices.why: It tried a hundred varied inputs.

choices.text: Because the property is written wrongly
choices.why: It is correct; it is simply true of this version.

choices.text: The last part absorbs the remainder
choices.why: Right. The bug is in how evenly it spreads, which the other property checks.

choices.text: Because round() always rounds down in Python
choices.why: Python rounds halves to the even number, which is how 0.5 became 0.
